title: Pressure in Fluids, Atmospheric Pressure and Upthrust
description: Pressure in a liquid column, why atmospheric pressure falls with altitude, and upthrust.
content_html:
Pressure in Fluids

A fluid is any substance that can flow — this includes both liquids and gases. A fluid at rest exerts pressure on any surface in contact with it. This pressure acts in all directions at any given point in the fluid.

Key Fact

Liquids and gases are both fluids. A fluid at rest pushes on every surface it touches, and at any point in the fluid that pressure acts in all directions.

Pressure in a Column of Liquid

The pressure in a fluid increases with depth. This is because the deeper you go, the greater the weight of the column of fluid above you. The equation for calculating pressure due to a column of liquid is:

Key Fact — Pressure in a Column of Liquid

\(p = h \times \rho \times g\), where p = pressure in pascals (Pa), h = height of the column in metres (m), ρ = density of the liquid in kg/m³, and g = gravitational field strength in N/kg (on Earth, g = 9.8 N/kg).

This equation tells us three factors that affect pressure in a liquid: the depth (height of the column), the density of the liquid, and the gravitational field strength. A denser liquid (such as mercury compared to water) produces a higher pressure at the same depth. Similarly, a greater depth means a taller column of liquid pressing down, creating more pressure.

Calculate the pressure exerted at the bottom of a swimming pool that is 2.5 m deep. The density of water is 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.8 N/kg.

Step 1: Write the equation: p = h × ρ × g

Step 2: Substitute: p = 2.5 × 1000 × 9.8

Step 3: Calculate: p = 24,500 Pa (or 24.5 kPa)

Atmospheric Pressure

Atmospheric pressure is the pressure exerted by the weight of the air above a surface. At sea level, atmospheric pressure is approximately 101 kPa (about 101,325 Pa). The atmosphere is a thin layer of gas attracted to the Earth by gravity.

As altitude increases, atmospheric pressure decreases. This is because at higher altitudes there is a shorter column of air above you, so there is less weight of air pressing down. The density of the atmosphere also decreases with altitude because gravity pulls gas molecules closer to the Earth’s surface, meaning fewer molecules are present at higher altitudes.

Key Fact

Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude because there is less air above to exert a downward force. At sea level it is about 101 kPa; on a mountaintop it is significantly lower.

Compare the atmospheric pressure at sea level with the atmospheric pressure at the top of a mountain. Explain the difference in terms of the air above each location.

Answer: Atmospheric pressure at sea level is higher than at the top of a mountain (1). At sea level there is a taller column of air above (1), and that taller column has a greater weight pressing down (1). At the top of a mountain the column of air above is shorter, so less weight presses down and the pressure is lower (1).

Atmospheric pressure works in the same way as the pressure in a liquid: the taller the column of air above you, the greater the pressure. The atmosphere does not have a clear boundary — it gradually thins out into space. This is why there is no sudden edge where atmospheric pressure drops to zero.

Upthrust and Floating

Upthrust is an upward force that acts on any object placed in a fluid. It is caused by the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the object. Because pressure increases with depth, the bottom of the object experiences a greater pressure (and therefore a greater force) than the top.

The result is a net upward force — the upthrust. Whether an object sinks or floats depends on how the upthrust compares to the object’s weight:

If the weight of the object is greater than the upthrust, the object sinks. This happens when the object is denser than the fluid it is placed in. If the weight is equal to the upthrust, the object floats. This happens when the object displaces a volume of fluid whose weight matches its own weight.

For example, a steel ship floats despite steel being denser than water because the hull is shaped to displace a large volume of water. The upthrust from this displaced water is enough to support the ship’s weight. A solid steel ball, however, sinks because it displaces a much smaller volume of water relative to its weight.

Consider a cube submerged in water. The pressure on the bottom face is greater than the pressure on the top face because the bottom is deeper. Since pressure = force ÷ area, and the top and bottom faces have the same area, the force on the bottom face is greater than the force on the top face. This difference in force is the upthrust.

The sideways pressures on the left and right (and front and back) faces are equal and opposite, so they cancel out. Only the vertical pressure difference produces a net force — the upthrust acting upward.

Key Fact

An object floats when the upthrust equals its weight. An object sinks when its weight exceeds the upthrust. Upthrust is caused by the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the object in a fluid.
exam_tip_html: This content is examined on Physics Paper 2, a written exam of 1 hour 45 minutes worth 100 marks. For calculation questions using p = hρg, always check your units — h must be in metres, ρ in kg/m³, and g in N/kg to get a pressure in pascals. For “explain” questions about pressure at depth or at altitude, write about the column of fluid above the point and the weight pressing down. For floating and sinking, compare the upthrust with the weight rather than only saying that something is “less dense”.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A fluid is any substance that can flow, so liquids and gases are both fluids. A fluid at rest pushes on every surface it touches, in all directions.
  • Pressure in a liquid increases with depth and depends on density and gravitational field strength: p = hρg. Atmospheric pressure is about 101 kPa at sea level and decreases with altitude because there is less air above.
  • Upthrust is the upward force on an object in a fluid, caused by the pressure difference between its top and bottom. An object floats when upthrust equals weight; it sinks when weight exceeds upthrust.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a fluid.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for:
• A substance that can flow / a liquid or a gas (1).

Accept: liquids and gases are both fluids.

practice_questions.text: A water tank is filled to a depth of 1.5 m. The density of water is 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.8 N/kg. Calculate the pressure at the bottom of the tank.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Correct substitution into p = h × ρ × g: p = 1.5 × 1000 × 9.8 (1)
• Correct answer: p = 14,700 Pa (or 14.7 kPa) (1)

Allow error carried forward if the substitution is correct but the arithmetic is wrong.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the pressure on a diver increases as they swim deeper into the sea.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• As depth increases, the height of the column of water above the diver increases (1)
• A taller column of water has a greater weight pressing down (1)
• Pressure is calculated using p = hρg, so greater h gives greater pressure (1)

Accept: reference to more water above / more fluid pressing down for the weight mark.

practice_questions.text: Compare the atmospheric pressure at sea level with the atmospheric pressure at the top of a mountain. Explain the difference in terms of the air above each location.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Atmospheric pressure at sea level is higher than at the top of a mountain (1)
• At sea level there is a taller column of air above (1)
• This taller column has a greater weight / more air molecules pressing down (1)
• At the top of a mountain, the column of air above is shorter / less air above, so there is less weight pressing down and pressure is lower (1)

Accept: reference to density of air being lower at altitude for the final mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe what causes the upthrust on a cube that is fully submerged in water.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• The bottom face is deeper, so the pressure on it is greater than the pressure on the top face (1)
• The two faces have the same area, so the force on the bottom face is greater than the force on the top face (1)
• This difference in force acts upwards and is the upthrust (1)

Accept: the sideways forces are equal and opposite, so they cancel.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a steel ship floats on water even though steel is denser than water. In your answer, refer to upthrust, weight, and the volume of water displaced.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Thorough, logically structured explanation linking upthrust to pressure difference, explaining how the hull shape displaces enough water, and correctly comparing upthrust to weight.
E.g. The hollow hull shape of the ship means it displaces a very large volume of water. The pressure at the bottom of the hull is greater than at the top because pressure increases with depth (p = hρg). This pressure difference creates an upward force called upthrust. The upthrust equals the weight of the water displaced. Because the hull displaces such a large volume, the weight of water displaced is enough to equal the total weight of the ship, so the ship floats. A solid block of steel would displace much less water relative to its weight, so it would sink.
Mid band (3-4): Correct reference to upthrust and displacement but limited explanation of pressure difference or incomplete comparison of upthrust and weight.
Lower band (1-2): Basic statements such as ‘the ship floats because of upthrust’ with little or no explanation of why.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the correct equation for pressure due to a column of liquid?
What happens to atmospheric pressure as altitude increases?
Atmospheric pressure at sea level is approximately _____ kPa.
Upthrust is caused by the _____ difference between the top and bottom of an object in a fluid.
Match each situation to what happens:
left: The upthrust equals the object’s weight
The object’s weight is greater than the upthrust
The same point is moved deeper into a liquid

flashcard_questions.a: Any substance that can flow, which covers liquids and gases.

flashcard_questions.q: (Higher) Why does pressure in a liquid increase with depth?
flashcard_questions.a: There is a greater weight of liquid in the column above.

flashcard_questions.q: (Higher) p = ____ × ____ × ____, the pressure in a column of liquid.
(Higher) How does the density of a liquid affect pressure at a given depth?
flashcard_questions.a: A denser liquid gives a higher pressure at the same depth.

flashcard_questions.q: What is atmospheric pressure at sea level?
Why does atmospheric pressure fall as altitude increases?
flashcard_questions.a: There is a shorter column of air above, so less weight presses down.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to the density of the atmosphere at high altitude?
flashcard_questions.a: It falls, because gravity holds the gas molecules closer to the surface.

flashcard_questions.q: (Higher) What causes the upthrust on an object in a fluid?
flashcard_questions.a: The pressure on its bottom face is greater than on its top face.

flashcard_questions.q: (Higher) When does an object float in a fluid?
flashcard_questions.a: When the upthrust equals its weight.

flashcard_questions.q: (Higher) When does an object sink in a fluid?
flashcard_questions.a: When its weight is greater than the upthrust.

flashcard_questions.q: (Higher) Why does a steel ship float even though steel is dense?
flashcard_questions.a: Its hull displaces a large volume of water, giving enough upthrust.

flashcard_questions.q: (Higher) Why do the sideways pressures on a submerged cube cancel out?
flashcard_questions.a: They are equal and opposite on the faces that face each other.

glossary_terms.definition: A substance that can flow — both liquids and gases are fluids.
Mass per unit volume of a substance, measured in kg/m³. Denser fluids create greater pressure at the same depth.
The pressure exerted by the weight of the atmosphere above a surface — approximately 101,325 Pa (about 101 kPa) at sea level.
The upward force exerted on an object submerged in a fluid, caused by the difference in pressure between the top and bottom of the object.
